facts.statement: Aussiedraco is a genus of pterosaur, which are flying reptiles.
facts.quote: Aussiedraco (meaning "Australian dragon") is a genus of pterosaur, an order of flying reptiles

facts.statement: Aussiedraco is known from a single fragment of a lower jawbone called a dentary.
facts.quote: It is known from a single dentary (lower jawbone) fragment

facts.statement: The fossil of Aussiedraco was first discovered in the 1970s in western Queensland.
facts.quote: This dentary was first discovered in the 1970s in a site in western Queensland

facts.statement: Aussiedraco was initially described in 1980 by Ralph E. Molnar and Richard A. Thulborn as belonging to the genus Ornithocheirus.
facts.quote: It was initially described in 1980 by Australian paleontologists Ralph E. Molnar and Richard A. Thulborn as belonging to Ornithocheirus

facts.statement: Before being recognized as a new genus, the Aussiedraco fossil was assigned to Ornithocheirus, Anhanguera, and Lonchodectes.
facts.quote: Until it was recognized as coming from its own genus and species, this dentary was assigned to Ornithocheirus, Anhanguera, and Lonchodectes

facts.statement: Aussiedraco molnari was scientifically described in 2011 by Alexander Kellner, Taissa Rodrigues, and Fabiana R. Costa.
facts.quote: In 2011, Brazilian paleontologists Alexander Kellner, Taissa Rodrigues, and Fabiana R. Costa scientifically described it as Aussiedraco molnari

facts.statement: Aussiedraco lived during the Early Cretaceous period in what is now Australia.
facts.quote: that lived during the Early Cretaceous in what is now Australia

facts.statement: During the Albian stage, the Toolebuc Formation where Aussiedraco lived was a near-shore open ocean with low oxygenated waters.
facts.quote: During the Albian the Toolebuc Formation was a near-land open ocean that had low oxygenated waters

facts.statement: Before 1980, no pterosaur material had been reported from Australia in scientific literature.
facts.quote: Prior to 1980, no pterosaur material had been reported form Australia in scientific literature

facts.statement: Aussiedraco fossils were unearthed in the 1970s from the Toolebuc Formation in western Queensland, Australia.
facts.quote: Fossils of Aussiedraco were first unearthed in the 1970s from a flaggy limestone outcrop of the Toolebuc Formation around 70 km east of Bouila and 13 km south of the Hamilton Hotel in western Queensland, Australia

facts.statement: The only known remains of Aussiedraco are an incomplete mandibular symphysis cataloged as specimen QM F10613 at the Queensland Museum.
facts.quote: The remains known of Aussiedraco consist of a single, incomplete mandibular symphysis (the area of the lower jaw where the left and right mandibles meet), which is cataloged at the Queensland Museum under specimen number QM F10613

facts.statement: Ralph E. Molnar and Richard A. Thulborn described specimen QM F10613 in the journal Nature in 1980.
facts.quote: In 1980, Australian paleontologists Ralph E. Molnar and Richard A. Thulborn described QM F10613 in an article in the journal Nature

facts.statement: In 2011, Kellner, Rodrigues, and Costa identified QM F10613 as a new species, Aussiedraco molnari.
facts.quote: In 2011, Brazilian paleontologists Alexander Kellner, Taissa Rodrigues, and Fabiana R. Costa scientifically described QM F10613 and identified it as belonging to a new genus and species of pternodontoid pterosaur, Aussiedraco molnari

facts.statement: Kellner and colleagues assigned Aussiedraco to the clade Pteranodontoidea.
facts.quote: In their description, Kellner and colleagues assigned Aussiedraco to the Pteranodontoidea, a clade roughly containing the same species as the Ornithocheiroidea sensu Unwin

facts.statement: Kellner and colleagues stated that Aussiedraco is closely allied with Anhangueridae but is not a member of it.
facts.quote: They further stated that it would be more closely allied with Anhangueridae, but would not itself be a member

facts.statement: In 2019, Rubi Pêgas and colleagues established the new group Targaryendraconia for toothed pterodactyloids.
facts.quote: In 2019, Brazilian paleontologist Rubi Pêgas and colleagues published a study in which they recognized a new cosmopolitan group of toothed pterodactyloids, which they termed Targaryendraconia

facts.statement: Targaryendraconia includes the families Cimoliopteridae and Targaryendraconidae, the latter containing Aussiedraco.
facts.quote: This clade includes two families: Cimoliopteridae, which includes genera like Cimoliopterus and Aetodactylus, and Targaryendraconidae, which includes Aussiedraco itself, Targaryendraco, and Barbosania

facts.statement: Pêgas and colleagues (2019) recovered Aussiedraco, Barbosania, and Targaryendraco as sister taxa.
facts.quote: In their phylogenetic analysis, Pêgas and colleagues (2019) recovered Aussiedraco, Barbosania, and Targaryendraco as sister taxa

facts.statement: The dentary of Aussiedraco is unique because it lacks crests, has a convex surface, and a flat bottom surface.
facts.quote: The dentary of Aussiedraco is very unique. It lacks any crests, bears a convex surface, and has a flat ventral (bottom) surface

facts.statement: The anatomy of Aussiedraco's tooth sockets suggests its bottom and top teeth could interlock.
facts.quote: Based on the anatomy of its alveoli (tooth sockets) the bottom and top teeth could interlock

facts.statement: Aussiedraco lived alongside the pterosaurs Mythunga, Ferrodraco, and Haliskia in the Toolebuc Formation.
facts.quote: Aussiedraco lived alongside the other pterosaurs Mythunga, Ferrodraco, and Haliskia in the Toolebuc Formation

facts.statement: Aussiedraco was named by Alexander W.A. Kellner, Taissa Rodrigues, and Fabiana R. Costa in 2011.
facts.quote: Fue nombrado por Alexander W.A. Kellner, Taissa Rodrigues y Fabiana R. Costa en el año de 2011

facts.statement: The genus name combines "Aussie," a shortened form of Australian, and "draco," the Latin word for dragon.
facts.quote: El nombre del género se deriva del término "Aussie", una forma acortada de la palabra australiano en inglés, y "draco", de la palabra latina que significa dragón.

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Aussiedraco molnari.
facts.quote: la especie tipo es Aussiedraco molnari

facts.statement: The species name honors Ralph E. Molnar, who described the specimen in 1980.
facts.quote: El nombre de la especie honra a Ralph E. Molnar, quien describió el ejemplar en 1980.

facts.statement: The holotype of Aussiedraco is the mandibular symphysis specimen QM F10613, housed at the Queensland Museum.
facts.quote: Aussiedraco es conocido del holotipo QM F10613, una sínfisis mandibular alojada en el Museo de Queensland

facts.statement: The holotype was recovered from the Toolebuc Formation, approximately 70 km east of Boulia in western Queensland.
facts.quote: recuperado de rocas de la formación Toolebuc, cerca de 70 km al este de Boulia, en el occidente de Queensland

facts.statement: The fossil dates to the Albian stage.
facts.quote: datando de la época del Albiense

facts.statement: The holotype fragment of the mandibular symphysis measures about 88 mm in length.
facts.quote: El fragmento de la sínfisis mide 88 milímetros de largo

facts.statement: Based on empty elliptical tooth sockets, the lower jaw likely carried at least five pairs of teeth.
facts.quote: Hasta donde se puede saber juzgando por sus alvéolos elípticos vacíos, la mandíbula inferior tenía al menos cinco pares de dientes

facts.statement: Aussiedraco is distinguished from all other pterosaurs by having a convex top mandibular margin and a straight bottom margin.
facts.quote: It is distinguished from all other pterosaurs by the presence of a convex dorsal (top) mandibular margin and a straight ventral (bottom) margin.

facts.statement: Aussiedraco possesses two folds on the tip of its lower jaw, a feature not found in other pterosaurs.
facts.quote: The most notably difference between the two genera is that Aussiedraco bears two sucli (folds) on its rostral mandibular tip.

facts.statement: Aussiedraco is an extinct basal ornithocheiroid pterodactyloid pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Australia.
facts.quote: Aussiedraco es un género extinto de pterosaurio pterodactiloide ornitoqueiroide basal de principios del Cretácico de Australia.

facts.statement: Aussiedraco lived between 106.3 and 100.5 million years ago during the Albian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Albian to Albian (106.3 to 100.5 million years ago)

facts.statement: Aussiedraco is classified as a reptile.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: The genus authority for Aussiedraco is Kellner, Rodrigues & Costa, 2011.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Kellner, Rodrigues & Costa, 2011

facts.statement: Kellner and colleagues assigned Aussiedraco to the clade Pteranodontoidea, which contains essentially the same species as Ornithocheiroidea.
facts.quote: Kellner e.a. asignó Aussiedraco a Pteranodontoidea, un clado que básicamente contiene las mismas especies que Ornithocheiroidea sensu Unwin.

facts.statement: Aussiedraco may be closely related to the family Anhangueridae.
facts.quote: Aussiedraco podría estar cercanamente relacionado con la familia Anhangueridae.

facts.statement: The scalloping of the tooth sockets suggests that the upper and lower teeth of Aussiedraco could interlock, particularly at the front margin.
facts.quote: Based on the scalloping of the alveoli, the upper and lower teeth were likely able to interlock, especially at the anterior (front) margin of the symphysis.

facts.statement: The first four tooth sockets are positioned vertically and forward, causing the teeth to project outward.
facts.quote: The first through fourth alveoli are placed more dorsoventrally (up and forward), causing them to project outwards.

facts.statement: The frontmost two pairs of tooth sockets in Aussiedraco are longer than those in Ferrodraco, indicating larger front teeth.
facts.quote: The mesiodistal (length of tooth going from the midline of the face to the end of the face) lengths of the frontmost two pairs of alveoli are also greater than those of Ferrodraco, indicating that the front teeth of Aussiedraco were larger than Ferrodraco's.

facts.statement: The two folds on the lower jaw tip of Aussiedraco are unique among pterosaurs but might be an artifact of fossil preparation or a split groove.
facts.quote: The most notably difference between the two genera is that Aussiedraco bears two sucli (folds) on its rostral mandibular tip. This characteristic is absent in all other pterosaurs, but may have been caused by over preparation of the fossils with acetic acid or may represent a split mandibular groove.

facts.statement: A 2006 study by André J. Veldmeijer and colleagues suggested ornithocheiromorphs like Aussiedraco likely had fish-eating diets based on aquatic habitats, interlocking teeth, and forward-facing eyes.
facts.quote: In a 2006 study, Dutch paleontologist André J. Veldmeijer and colleagues stated ornithocheiromorphs likely had piscivorous diets due to their prevalence in aquatic habitats, interlocking teeth, and anteriorly-placed eyes.

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesized that ornithocheiromorphs hunted small fish or swallowed them after pre-digestion because their teeth lacked chewing adaptations.
facts.quote: Instead, they potentially hunted small fish or pre-digested them prior to swallowing, as their teeth lacked adaptations for chewing.

facts.statement: In 2012, Mark Witton suggested that the protruding sharp teeth at the front of ornithocheiromorph jaws were specialized for catching prey from water without landing.
facts.quote: In 2012, British paleontologist Mark Witton pointed out that the protruded, sharp teeth at the anterior tips of ornithocheiromorph jaws could have been specialized for catching prey from the water without landing.

facts.statement: The Toolebuc Formation was deposited at the southern edge of the Toolebuc Sea, which had deep anaerobic waters to the north and shallow aerobic brackish waters to the south.
facts.quote: The Toolebuc Formation was deposited in the southern edge of a late Albian Toolebuc Sea, which featured an anaerobic, relatively deep-water marine environment to the north and an aerobic, shallow-water marine and brackish environment to the south.

facts.statement: Isolated postcranial remains including shoulder girdles, vertebrae, and wing parts have been found in the Toolebuc Formation, though their assignment to Aussiedraco remains unconfirmed.
facts.quote: Many isolated pterosaur postcranial remains have been found from the Toolebuc Formation as well, such as a scapulocoracoid (shoulder girdle), vertebrae (backbones), and wing remains.

facts.statement: It is currently impossible to confirm if isolated postcranial remains from the Toolebuc Formation belong to Aussiedraco due to a lack of overlapping material.
facts.quote: These could belong to Aussiedraco, but the lack of overlap means this is impossible to confirm until more material is known.

facts.statement: While the unique jaw folds of Aussiedraco resemble those of Cearadactylus, suggesting they might be the same taxon, this is unlikely given the lack of confirmation and their different origins.
facts.quote: The only other pterosaur this is known from is Cearadactylus, a synonym of Brasileodactylus, suggesting that they may be synonyms (the same taxon). However, this is unlikely as this trait has not been confirmed and the two come from different terminals, continents, and families.

facts.statement: The ecology and diet of Aussiedraco and similar ornithocheiromorphs remain debated topics among scientists.
facts.quote: The ecology and diet of ornithocheiromorphs like Aussiedraco has been debated.

facts.statement: The holotype is a three-dimensionally preserved fragment about 88 mm long with a lightly built internal structure and thin bone cortex typical of pterosaurs.
facts.quote: The holotype consists of a three-dimensionally preserved fragment measuring about 88 mm in length. Internally it is lightly built with a thin bone cortex, as in other pterosaurs.

facts.statement: The holotype lacks a keel or crest, is convex on top with a narrow deep groove that does not reach the tip, but is flat on the bottom.
facts.quote: Carece de quilla o cresta y es convexo en la parte superior, con una media estrecha ranura profunda que no alcanza la punta, pero es plana en la parte inferior.

facts.statement: Aussiedraco is estimated to be smaller than Mythunga, another pterosaur from the same formation.
facts.quote: Se estima que Ausiedraco era menor en tamaño que Mythunga, un pterosaurio de la misma formación.
